text:
The passage rewards the reader who attends to what it leaves out. Sarah appears nowhere in the chapter, and her death is announced in the verse which immediately follows it. The scene implies, though it never states, that something in that household did not survive the mountain. The narrator turns away at the precise moment when a lesser story-teller would have lingered, and his silence is itself a kind of testimony; for when Abraham returns to the servants, of Isaac nothing whatever is said.

It may be objected that the chapter merely follows the conventions of ancient narrative, which rarely reports what its persons feel and never explains. This may, in some sense, be granted. The reticence here is nevertheless deliberate. The narrator knows what he is about, and restraint in his hands becomes a kind of accusation; for he is elsewhere ready enough to report what passes within his persons: Esau cries out, Jacob is afraid, Joseph weeps.
